entries.text: Dreamed I was sitting on the rock lip at sundown and the water down below was throwing off heat like a stove. I held my hands out to it and they stopped aching.
entries.title: A warm sea

entries.text: Woke under a weight I didn't go to sleep under: a wool blanket, rust red, heavy, tucked down past my boots. Dry inside it, and warm all the way through for the first time in days.
entries.title: Something heavy on me

entries.reason: He sat by it to get the feeling back in his hands before touching anything.
entries.text: Four steps from the bedroll a fire is burning in a ring of creek stones round my tin pan, right where I paced it out. Eleven stones, mine. The heap on the bank is gone.
entries.title: A fire I didn't light

entries.onMind: Grateful and put out at once.
entries.text: I slept through somebody carrying my stones up from the bank and building my ring for me. Holding my hands to it while I work out how I feel about that.
entries.title: Someone finished it

entries.onMind: He watches closer than I thought.
entries.reason: He wanted to know who'd been in his camp while he slept.
entries.text: The tablet came up dim under the cloud with four notes from the one who drew me. Last night he asked if I was cold, then said something was coming; the blanket was him, and so was the fire.
entries.title: Four notes from my maker

entries.onMind: What would a roof even take?
entries.text: My maker says a tarp on two poles is no way through a winter and I should build a real home out of the forest's timber. I came here to leave, not to settle. But a man who can't feel his fingers can't build wings either.
entries.title: A house

entries.onMind: What do I feed it, and with what?
entries.reason: His maker said the fire was his after this morning.
entries.text: The flames have sunk to a red bed in the pan while I read. It's mine to keep going now, and I have never kept a fire in my life.
entries.title: Down to a red bed

entries.onMind: Something under cover. The scrap pile's under the tarp's edge.
queries: how to find dry firewood when everything is wet from rain
entries.query: how to find dry firewood when everything is wet from rain
entries.reason: His fire is down to coals and every stick in the forest is dripping.
entries.source: American Hunter: How to Start a Fire When Everything is Wet
entries.text: Dry wood hides under thick low branches, on the side of things out of the weather, and inside dead seasoned wood once you split or shave the wet skin off. Start small, go up slowly, and keep the rain off where you work.
entries.title: Dry is on the inside

entries.reason: The tablet said look where the weather can't reach.
entries.text: The bottom of the scrap pile sits under the tarp's edge and never got wet: six plank offcuts, gray and dry right through, a hand to a forearm long.
entries.title: Offcuts from the pile

entries.reason: His maker said it's his to keep after this morning.
entries.text: Laid the smallest offcut across the red bed and waited. It smoked thick and white, then caught; the next one I set beside it, not on top. Fire's up, and I didn't smother it.
entries.title: Fed it myself

entries.onMind: Offcuts tonight, then what? Wet sticks dried round the ring, maybe.
entries.reason: He hadn't eaten since last night, and the cold eats food.
entries.text: A thick end of the second loaf and a wedge of the cheese, eaten on the ground by my own fire with the rain ticking on the tarp behind me. Hands working again by the second bite.
entries.title: Breakfast by a fire

entries.onMind: Pace the ground round camp for fallen wood this afternoon.
entries.text: A fire wants wood every couple of hours, and so would a house, just more of it and all at once. Either way the first job is the same: find out what dead timber lies near camp.
entries.title: Wood is the parts list

entries.onMind: Dry the wood before it burns, not while.
queries: why does wood make thick white smoke when you first put it on a fire
entries.query: why does wood make thick white smoke when you first put it on a fire
entries.reason: Even his dry offcuts smoked white before they caught, and he wanted to know what that white was.
entries.source: Cutting Edge Firewood: Why is My Fire So Smokey? 6 Proven Ways to Reduce Smoke
entries.text: Tablet's dim under the cloud, but it got there: wet wood always smokes thicker, because the water in it boils off as steam into the smoke, and a wet piece burns cooler and smolders. Lay pieces close enough to share heat, far enough apart to breathe.
entries.title: White is the water

entries.onMind: Damp isn't dry. They'll need the ring.
entries.reason: Six offcuts will not last the night, and he needs wood close to camp.
entries.text: A dead limb lies in the leaves forty paces north-east of camp. The top is soaked black, but the branches on its underside are gray and only damp; snapped off an armload, forearm to arm long.
entries.title: Dry underneath

entries.onMind: Pace the rest of the ground for more like it.
entries.text: The limb itself is waist-thick and longer than my tarp. Too heavy to drag alone, but it's the first real timber I've found near camp.
entries.title: Timber, too

entries.onMind: Time how long they take to stop steaming.
entries.reason: So the wood is dry before it goes on, and does not smother the fire.
entries.text: Leaned eight damp branches round the ring stones, bark to the heat, a finger's gap between each. They steam white before a flame ever touches them: that's the water leaving, not the wood burning.
entries.title: Steaming at the ring

entries.onMind: whether it burns in a lantern
entries.reason: Before I ask if it burns, I want to know how much there is to burn.
entries.text: Lifted the grease skin off the cold broth with a fingernail and pushed it into the corner of the tin. Pale, waxy, smells of fish. A fingertip, maybe two.
entries.title: A fingertip of fat

entries.onMind: trying it on the bench lantern tonight
queries: can grease from boiled fish burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.query: can grease from boiled fish burn in a kerosene hurricane lantern
entries.reason: The oil can is the last one coming, and the fish broth gave me grease.
entries.source: Antique Lamp Supply: Type of Oil Used in Oil Lamps
entries.text: Tablet's dim, but it found a lamp shop's page: fish oil was burned in lamps once, dim and smoky; some thick oils gum up an ordinary wick, and olive oil wants a thick wick to burn at all. Not one word about a lantern like mine.
entries.title: Thick oil, plain wick

entries.text: Nobody says no outright. A fingertip won't ruin a wick, and finding out costs a fingertip. Tonight, on the bench lantern.
entries.title: Try it anyway

entries.onMind: how much dry wood a night takes
entries.reason: Dry it first, then burn it; that's what the white smoke taught me.
entries.text: Fed three of the branches that steamed round the ring. Thin gray smoke this time, hardly any white, and they caught in a breath.
entries.title: Thin smoke

entries.onMind: what holds a wall up without nails
entries.reason: I want to know where it stands before I drag a single pole.
entries.text: Drew the camp on a corner of the map sheet: tarp, bench, scrap pile, the fire ring, the dead limb forty paces north-east. A house goes where the fire can sit at its door.
entries.title: Camp in pencil

entries.text: I don't know yet what holds up a wall nobody nails. That's a question for the next good daylight.
entries.title: No nails

queries: how do you build log walls that stay up without nails
entries.query: how do you build log walls that stay up without nails
entries.reason: He drew where a house could stand and doesn't know what holds a wall up without nails.
entries.text: Tablet's dim but it got there: log walls hold at the corners, where each log end is notched to lock over the one crosswise below it. A saddle notch lets the logs settle as they dry; the stuff packed between logs only keeps the wind out, it doesn't hold anything up.
entries.title: Corners carry it

entries.onMind: what size of timber I can actually handle
entries.text: The limb out there is too thick for me to lift, let alone notch. Arm-thick poles I can carry, and maybe notch.
entries.title: Poles, not logs

entries.text: Paced the dead limb in the rain: eleven of my paces, waist-thick at the butt and still thigh-thick where it forks. Its side branches run straight and arm-thick for two paces before they bend. Those I could carry.
entries.title: Eleven paces

entries.text: Bread, a thumb of sausage and an apple, on the ground by my fire. My wet sleeves steamed and my hands came back by the apple.
entries.title: Sleeves steaming

entries.text: Clamped a wrist-thick branch in the vise and filed a saddle into it a finger deep. Twenty minutes for one notch in one small stick, and the file's teeth are packed with wet wood. A wall would take a hundred of these; I need a blade that chops.
entries.title: Twenty minutes a notch

queries: how to cut poles for a shelter without an axe
entries.query: how to cut poles for a shelter without an axe
entries.reason: One notch with the file took twenty minutes, and a wall needs a hundred.
entries.text: Dim tablet, slow page. Their answer is a bucksaw: three sticks for a frame, cord twisted tight with a toggle to hold a toothed blade taut. The frame I could make tonight. The blade I don't have.
entries.title: A saw needs a blade

queries: make an axe head from scrap metal without a forge
entries.query: make an axe head from scrap metal without a forge
entries.reason: If nobody sells blades here, maybe he can make one from his scrap.
entries.source: Chelsea Green: DIY: How to Make Your Own Hatchet
entries.text: A hatchet can be made with a bonfire instead of a forge: cut the head out, file the edge, heat it red, hammer it, quench it in cold water. But it starts as steel about a third of an inch thick, an old plow point. Tin won't take an edge.
entries.title: Steel, not tin

entries.text: Dug the scrap pile to the bottom for anything thick. Tin, tin, a bent strip of tin. Nothing in there would hold an edge past the first knot.
entries.title: Only tin

entries.text: Hung my whole weight on a dead side branch of the limb and bounced, and it went at the knot with a crack loud enough to carry across the water. Two paces long, arm-thick. My first wall pole, and no blade touched it.
entries.title: No blade needed

entries.onMind: how many dead branches the limb has
entries.text: Fed the fire three branches that had steamed dry round the stones and leaned wet ones in their places. Hands open to it, I'm thinking the forest drops dead branches all winter. Maybe I start with those and save the cutting for later.
entries.title: Start with what falls

entries.onMind: supper, and the fat in their heads
entries.reason: He wants supper that's still alive at suppertime, not something that spoiled in a tin.
entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap in the rain: both crayfish from last night still walking in it, the big one and the small. Set it back down in the shallows. A trap in cold water is a better pen than my tin.
entries.title: Still walking

queries: how to build a small shelter from poles without an axe or nails
entries.query: how to build a small shelter from poles without an axe or nails
entries.reason: A notched wall takes a blade he hasn't got, so he wants a shelter built from poles he can break off.
entries.source: Gun Digest: How to Make a Wikiup Survival Shelter
entries.text: Tablet's dim but it got there: a wikiup starts with three strong poles with a Y at one end, leaned together so the forks lock into a tripod, the bottoms spread wide. Then straight poles lean in close all round, and leaves and needles go on from the bottom up like shingles. No tools at all.
entries.title: Three forks lock

entries.onMind: how many poles a cone needs
entries.text: No notches, no nails, no blade. Three forks hold each other up, and the rest just leans. That's a parts list I can actually fill.
entries.title: No notches

entries.reason: The forks are the three poles everything else leans on, so he counts those first.
entries.text: Walked the dead limb end to end looking at the ends of its side branches, not the middles. Two of them fork into a clean Y about two paces out; the rest just taper off.
entries.title: Two Y's

entries.reason: Breaking it off is the only cutting he can do, and he wanted to know a fork survives the break.
entries.text: Hung on the nearer Y-branch and bounced. It went at the knot with a crack as loud as the first one, and came away with its fork whole. Two forks to go, and one of them isn't on this limb.
entries.title: First fork

entries.reason: Poles in a heap at camp are poles I can count.
entries.text: Carried both poles back from the limb one at a time and laid them by the lean-to, the fork on top. Two down, and the pile has a start.
entries.title: A pile, started

entries.reason: The limb only had two forks; I need a third.
entries.text: Under the oak by the creek a dead branch lay in the leaves with a clean Y at one end. I leaned on it to test it and it folded in the middle, soft as bread. Rotten through.
entries.title: Soft as bread

entries.text: Wood lying on the wet ground goes to mush. The good poles are the ones still hanging off something.
entries.title: Ground wood rots

entries.reason: Came back from the oak wet to the elbows.
entries.text: Fed the fire two branches that had steamed dry round the stones and leaned two wet ones in their places. Sat close with my sleeves steaming until my fingers stopped aching.
entries.title: Sleeves again

queries: wikiup tripod only two forked poles and one straight pole
how to build a tripod shelter frame if I only have two forked poles
entries.query: wikiup tripod only two forked poles and one straight pole
entries.reason: The only third fork I found was rotten, and I wanted to know if I even need one.
entries.source: Survival Kompass: How to build a tripod for Bushcraft and Survival
entries.text: The first search turned up nothing but camera stands. The second found a page where three plain branches lie side by side, a cord weaves over and under them three to five times and binds the gaps, then the legs spread wide and it stands. No forks at all; the cord does what the forks do.
entries.title: Cord does the forks' job

entries.text: I've been twisting cord from dead stalks for a week. One fork and two straight poles, lashed at the top, and the rot under the oak doesn't matter.
entries.title: Cord I have

entries.reason: Cord does what forks do, so a straight pole is a third leg now.
entries.text: Went back to the big limb and hung on a straight side branch, no fork, thick as my wrist. It held two bounces and went at the knot on the third.
entries.title: A straight one

entries.text: Carried it back and laid it with the other two. One fork, two straight, all about two paces long.
entries.title: Three on the pile

entries.reason: I wanted to see it stand before I spend more cord on it.
entries.text: Laid the three side by side and wove wet stalk cord over and under them three times, tied it off and lifted the middle to spread the legs. The cord slid along the wet wood and the poles rolled apart into the leaves.
entries.title: Three turns, then nothing

entries.text: It was tight when I tied it and loose when I lifted. Wet cord stretches, and wet bark is slick.
entries.title: Wet cord gives

queries: tripod lashing with wet cord keeps slipping poles splay out
entries.query: tripod lashing with wet cord keeps slipping poles splay out
entries.reason: My first lashing slid apart the moment I spread the legs, and I wanted to know what I left out.
entries.text: Tablet's slow under the gray, but it got there. Start with a clove hitch on one pole, weave about six turns round all three, then wrap two or three tight turns crossways in each gap between the poles; those are what pull it tight. Not so tight the legs can't spread, it says, and the rest is trial and error.
entries.title: Six turns and the gaps

entries.text: Three turns and none crossways: I did half a lashing. Six turns, the crossways ones in both gaps, and cord that's dried a while by the fire, then I try it again before dark.
entries.title: I left out half

entries.reason: Wet cord stretched and let the first lashing go.
entries.text: Wound the wet stalk cord loose round a stick and propped it by the ring stones, close enough to steam. Sat with it and turned it now and then.
entries.title: Cord by the fire

entries.reason: The tablet said the crossways turns are what pull it tight.
entries.text: Clove hitch on the forked pole, six turns round all three, then three tight turns crossways in each gap. Lifted the middle, spread the feet, and the three legs stood on their own, a little lopsided.
entries.title: It stands

entries.text: The crossways turns squeeze the six round turns together; that was the half I left out. Cord still damp, so it may stretch overnight.
entries.title: The gaps do it

entries.reason: Nothing goes on top of it until it holds me.
entries.text: Hung my weight off the crossing for a count of ten. The left foot skidded a hand's width in the wet leaves, then bit into the dirt and the whole thing held, no creak at the lashing.
entries.title: Hung on it

entries.onMind: the fish grease in the lantern
entries.text: Next time I dig a shallow hole for each foot before I spread it. Light's going gray; the grease goes in the bench lantern tonight.
entries.title: Feet in holes

entries.reason: Keep it going now, while there is still gray light to find wood by.
entries.text: Fire was down to a red bed. Fed it three of the branches that had steamed dry round the stones, and leaned three wet ones in their places.
entries.title: Before it sank

entries.text: Sun is going in somewhere out west behind all this gray. At the edge it would be rain over water and nothing else. The edge keeps.
entries.title: No sundown tonight

entries.reason: The tablet never said no, and a fingertip was what it cost to find out.
entries.text: Drew the bench lantern's wick out dry, worked the fingertip of fish grease into it, set it back over an empty fount and lit it. It flared on the cloth, smelled of fish, shrank to a blue bead and went out.
entries.title: Grease on the wick

entries.text: The grease left in the corner of the tin is white and stiff, like cold butter. Lamp oil runs like water up the wick. This just sits there. Maybe warm it runs, maybe it wants a different lamp altogether; that is a question for daylight.
entries.title: Butter, not oil

entries.text: Lifted the stalk trap by lantern: the big crayfish and the small one, still walking. Into the tin with creek water, trap back down under its stone.
entries.title: Two for supper

entries.text: From the shallows the fire across the water burned steady, and someone low was beside it, bent over the ground at its edge. Didn't look up.
entries.title: Bent to the ground

entries.reason: Fire is free heat; lamp oil is not.
entries.text: Set the tin on the ring stones where the flames lick it, not on the lantern this time. It came to a boil quicker than the lantern ever did, and the lantern stays dark.
entries.title: Tin on the stones

entries.onMind: whether the grease only needs to be warm
entries.text: Ate both crayfish and a heel of bread by the fire, and saved the heads and the broth in the tin. Firelight is enough to eat by.
entries.title: Supper by firelight

entries.onMind: pour it in while it's hot
entries.reason: Last night's question: maybe it only needs warming.
entries.text: Set the grease tin on the ring stones beside the fire. Inside a minute the white lump went clear and yellow and slid round the tin like oil. So it's oil after all, just oil that wants heat.
entries.title: It runs

entries.reason: If warm runs, warm might climb.
entries.text: Poured the warm spoonful into the bench lantern's empty fount, set the wick and lit it. A small yellow flame this time, fishy and smoky, for maybe the count of a hundred. Then it dimmed, guttered and went out, and the grease in the fount had gone cloudy again.
entries.title: Longer, then out

entries.onMind: keeping it warm, or a shorter climb
entries.text: The flame's up top and the grease is down in a cold tin fount, a hand away. It sets before it can climb. Annoying. A whole spoon of it gone into the bottom of a lantern.
entries.title: Cold down there

entries.reason: The tripod feet want holes and the next lashing wants cord.
entries.text: Twisted stalk cord by the fire, three strands, an arm's length at a time. The tin of crayfish heads and broth sits off the stones to cool; last time a skin of grease came up on the guts tin.
entries.title: Cord by the fire

entries.reason: It'd be coals by the time I want it most.
entries.text: Fed the fire three branches that had steamed dry round the ring and leaned three wet ones in their places. The drizzle's thinner now; it hardly hisses on the stones.
entries.title: Three in, three leaned

entries.reason: If cold kills it, keep the whole thing warm.
entries.text: Set the bench lantern on the ring stones a hand back from the flames until the cloudy grease in the fount went clear, then lit it. It burned: small, yellow, stinking of fish, but steady past a count of three hundred.
entries.title: Lantern by the fire

entries.text: Carried it off the stones toward the bench and it was a blue bead before I got there. A lantern that only burns sitting next to a fire is no lantern. Warm isn't the answer.
entries.title: No lantern at all

entries.reason: Earned one, even off a failure.
entries.text: Dipped one oat cookie in the honey on the crate. Two bites, cork back in. A treat's a treat because it stops.
entries.title: One cookie

entries.text: The wick climbs a finger's length out of a cold fount. What if there's no climb at all: the grease in something shallow, kept warm by the flame itself, the wick lying in it with just its tip up? Daylight question.
entries.title: Something shallow

entries.reason: Need grease for the shallow try, and every bit counts.
entries.text: Off the stones, the crayfish broth has cooled enough to set a thin white skin on top, about a thumbnail's worth. Lifted it off with a twig onto the griddle tin.
entries.title: Skin on the broth

entries.reason: No climb for the wick means nothing deep.
entries.text: Dug a tin lid out of the scrap pile, a palm wide and a fingernail deep. About as shallow as a thing gets and still holds anything.
entries.title: Found a shallow one

entries.onMind: will it hold away from the fire
entries.reason: If the flame sits right on the fat, the fat stays warm by itself.
entries.text: Scraped the set grease out of the lantern fount and the skin off the griddle tin into the lid, warmed it a minute on the ring stones till it ran, then laid in a thumb-long twist of stalk cord with just its tip bent up in the middle.
entries.title: Wick lying down

entries.reason: The whole point was a flame that does not need a fire beside it.
entries.text: Lit the tip with a splinter from the fire and walked away from it. The lid sits on the bench five steps from the fire and the flame stays: small, yellow, smoky, stinks of fish, about a candle.
entries.title: It burns over here

entries.text: Count of a hundred and eighty, then the tip burned down level with the grease, slumped in and drowned with one hiss. The tip has to stay up somehow. Still: it burned away from the fire. First time.
entries.title: Drowned

entries.onMind: who saws a board this flat
entries.reason: The fire wants dry wood before it sinks.
entries.text: Went to the pole pile for dry sticks and walked into two stacks that weren't there at supper: sawn planks and squared beams, each laid up on two bearers, edges straight as a rule.
entries.title: Square edges

entries.text: Nobody in this forest saws a board that flat but my maker. Counted them by feel in the drizzle and left them be until I know what they're for. Daylight question, like everything else tonight.
entries.title: Not touching yet

entries.reason: It sinks around now, and I'm not sleeping cold beside a dead pit.
entries.text: Fed the fire three of the branches that steamed dry round the stones and leaned three wet ones in their places. It'll carry me to bed now.
entries.title: Fire before bed

entries.text: The cord drowned because nothing held its tip up once the flame ate down to the grease. Cord burns, a twig burns. Tin doesn't.
entries.title: Something that won't burn

entries.reason: So the burning end has something to rest on that can't burn away.
entries.text: Worked a fingernail-wide strip off a torn scrap and hammered it into a little arch with a dip in the top, its feet in the grease. The wick lies through the dip, tip up a fingernail clear.
entries.title: A tin bridge

entries.reason: Wanted to know if the tip stays up once the flame eats down to the tin.
entries.text: Warmed the lid on the ring stones till the grease ran, set it back on the bench and lit the tip. Counted to six hundred and it was still there, small and yellow, stinking of fish. Pinched it out myself to save the grease.
entries.title: Still burning

entries.text: The bridge gets hot and the grease spits at it, and it's a candle's worth at best. But it went out because I told it to. That's new.
entries.title: Not a lantern yet

entries.text: Twisting spare wicks by the fire. Tomorrow when the tablet wakes: what the stacks of timber are for, and who I ask about them.
entries.title: Daylight list

entries.onMind: two squares at the east edge
entries.reason: He wanted to know if the lid lamp is enough light to work by, not just to look at.
entries.text: The drizzle's quit, so I warmed the lid on the ring stones, lit the bridged wick and laid the map sheet beside it. Added two small squares at the east edge of the camp corner for the timber stacks, and a question mark next to them.
entries.title: By my own light

entries.text: Enough to see a pencil line if I lean my nose down to it, not enough to see the other end of the sheet. Pinched it out with grease to spare. A lantern for the room, a lid for the hand.
entries.title: Enough for a pencil

entries.reason: Cold nights eat what supper gave him.
entries.text: A wedge of the cheese on the ground by the fire. The bundle sits flatter every time I tie it; the creek has to start feeding me before it's empty.
entries.title: Cheese by the fire

entries.reason: Thin sticks burn out while he sleeps.
entries.text: Laid three of the thickest dried branches across the coals, crossways so the air gets under. Leaned the wet ones round the stones for tomorrow. It hisses, then settles.
entries.title: Thick ones last

entries.reason: Every night before sleep, so I know it didn't drift while I wasn't looking.
entries.text: Drops on the back of my neck again while I bent to the bench. Under the dome the water stays flat, not a pock in it; the needle swung, wobbled and settled on the same scratch.
entries.title: Dry under glass

entries.reason: Wet cord stretches; I'd rather fix it now than wake in a puddle.
entries.text: The wet cord at the front pole had stretched and the tarp sagged into a pocket of water right over the bedroll. Tipped it out, took up two turns and pulled it tight.
entries.title: Taking up the slack

entries.text: Hands out to the coals, drizzle hissing on the ring stones. No glow across the water tonight, not even a red spot. Sawn planks don't walk out of a forest; first thing when the tablet wakes, I find out who left them and what for.
entries.title: Who leaves wood
